Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

I'm dating the NoProp43 site from its late-October 2026 items, a PPIC poll and a housing-groups release, so I'm guessing it's around the turn of October into November. CalMatters' October 5 date and an October 23 SF Chronicle editorial fit that window too, and I'm trying to pin down the current date from them.

I'm checking the latest PPIC October 2026 poll on Proposition 43, since the site cites a release calling its support "in freefall," and I'm also trying to trace the No side's claim that it would cost California communities nearly $3 billion a year to its source.

I'm checking the Media endorsements next: the Southern California News Group, the San Diego Union-Tribune, and the Mercury News back Proposition 43, while the Sacramento Bee opposes it. Since the editorial boards split both ways, this looks more like a values question than a settled one, and I'm about to search for the PPIC data on the measure.

In The Final Week of the General Election Campaign, A New PPIC Poll Shows 55% of Voters Surveyed Oppose Prop 43, With Just 42% In Support
SACRAMENTO, CA – With Election Day less than a week away, a new PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) finds Prop 43 falling far short of a majority. Opposition among likely voters has grown to 55%, up from 51% in PPIC’s September survey. Prop 43 now trails by 13 points.
“This poll confirms what we're hearing across the state: the more voters learn about Prop 43, the less they like it," said David Kaufman, No on Prop 43 campaign manager. "Opposition has climbed to 55 percent since September, and with ballots already coming in, voters are turning against a measure that would make it harder for their communities to fund firefighters, 911 response, and local services. Firefighters, nurses, teachers, healthcare leaders, and housing advocates have carried that message for months, and it's breaking through. We're not taking anything for granted. Between now and November 3, we're reaching every undecided voter we can."
WHAT’S AT STAKE :
Slower 911 response. Prop 43 makes it harder to fund local fire departments, meaning fewer firefighters and longer waits in an emergency.
Worse wildfire protection. Communities could lose the ability to staff and equip fire stations before the next major fire hits.
$3 billion each year: If Prop 43 had been the law, California communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year in funding for firefighters, 911 response, childcare, homelessness solutions, street repair, parks, and libraries.
A minority gets the final say. One-third of voters could block what two-thirds of their community wants.

In The Final Week of the General Election Campaign, A New PPIC Poll Shows 55% of Voters Surveyed Oppose Prop 43, With Just 42% In Support
SACRAMENTO, CA – With Election Day less than a week away, a new PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) finds Prop 43 falling far short of a majority. Opposition among likely voters has grown to 55%, up from 51% in PPIC’s September survey. Prop 43 now trails by 13 points.
“This poll confirms what we're hearing across the state: the more voters learn about Prop 43, the less they like it," said David Kaufman, No on Prop 43 campaign manager. "Opposition has climbed to 55 percent since September, and with ballots already coming in, voters are turning against a measure that would make it harder for their communities to fund firefighters, 911 response, and local services. Firefighters, nurses, teachers, healthcare leaders, and housing advocates have carried that message for months, and it's breaking through. We're not taking anything for granted. Between now and November 3, we're reaching every undecided voter we can."
WHAT’S AT STAKE :
Slower 911 response. Prop 43 makes it harder to fund local fire departments, meaning fewer firefighters and longer waits in an emergency.
Worse wildfire protection. Communities could lose the ability to staff and equip fire stations before the next major fire hits.
$3 billion each year: If Prop 43 had been the law, California communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year in funding for firefighters, 911 response, childcare, homelessness solutions, street repair, parks, and libraries.
A minority gets the final say. One-third of voters could block what two-thirds of their community wants.

Opposition among likely voters has grown to 55%, up from 51% in PPIC’s September survey. Prop 43 now trails by 13 points.
“This poll confirms what we're hearing across the state: the more voters learn about Prop 43, the less they like it," said David Kaufman, No on Prop 43 campaign manager. "Opposition has climbed to 55 percent since September, and with ballots already coming in, voters are turning against a measure that would make it harder for their communities to fund firefighters, 911 response, and local services. Firefighters, nurses, teachers, healthcare leaders, and housing advocates have carried that message for months, and it's breaking through. We're not taking anything for granted. Between now and November 3, we're reaching every undecided voter we can."
WHAT’S AT STAKE :
Slower 911 response. Prop 43 makes it harder to fund local fire departments, meaning fewer firefighters and longer waits in an emergency.
Worse wildfire protection. Communities could lose the ability to staff and equip fire stations before the next major fire hits.
$3 billion each year: If Prop 43 had been the law, California communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year in funding for firefighters, 911 response, childcare, homelessness solutions, street repair, parks, and libraries.
A minority gets the final say. One-third of voters could block what two-thirds of their community wants.

California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Daniella Segura, USA TODAY NETWORK
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 6:45 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass. That’s the point, say anti-tax advocates

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.

In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.

Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. 

Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.

Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. 

But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.

Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.

Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Daniella Segura, USA TODAY NETWORK
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 6:45 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? **What It Would Do:** Require a two-thirds majority to pass local special purpose tax measures placed on the ballot via citizen petition.
Currently in California, a local special purpose tax (a tax whose revenue is dedicated to a specific purpose, like child care) requires a simple majority to pass if the measure is placed on the ballot via citizen petition (a citizen-led campaign that collects signatures from qualified voters to get on the ballot).
Special purpose taxes that are placed on the ballot by a government entity, like a city or county council, require a two-thirds majority to pass.
Proposition 43 would amend the California Constitution and require that **all** future local special purpose taxes, regardless of how they are placed on the ballot, earn a two-thirds majority yes vote to pass.
The proposition threatens the ability of communities to create voter-approved children’s funds in the future by requiring these ballot measures to get more than 66% of the vote.
